spans.text: This book is built on one core belief: kids learn digital skills best when they're actually making something. The subtitle says it plainly: build, code, create. Safety travels alongside every project, introduced at the moment it's relevant, not as a separate lecture.

Not watching someone else make something. Not reading about how something works. Making it themselves: a drawing, a game, a webpage, a video. That act of creation is where real understanding happens. Safety knowledge sticks the same way: not as a list of rules to memorize, but as something built alongside every project, step by step.

That's the approach here. Each chapter in this book is organized around a project the reader builds. The skills and safety lessons travel alongside the work, introduced at the moment they're actually relevant. A child learning to publish a webpage for the first time is far more receptive to a conversation about privacy settings than a child reading about privacy in the abstract.
Who This Book Is For

This book is written for children ages eight through twelve. It assumes no prior experience with digital tools, coding, or web design. Every concept is introduced from the ground up. The projects scale in complexity as the book progresses, so a child who works through the chapters in order will build real competence by the end, not just surface familiarity.

The reading level is designed for independent use by confident readers around ages ten through twelve. For children ages eight through ten, or for any child who prefers guided learning, reading alongside an adult makes the experience richer. Many families and classrooms will find the projects work best as shared activities.
What Your Child Will Build
By the time a reader completes this book, they will have:
- Set up an organized digital workspace and created a personal Digital Rules Poster
- Built a file organization system and reviewed privacy settings on their accounts
- Created an original piece of digital art and planned an illustrated story
- Coded an animated sprite in Scratch that moves, bounces, and responds to clicks
- Built a complete maze game in Scratch with keyboard controls, wall detection, scoring, and a timer
- Published a real webpage with original content and a designed layout
- Planned and begun their Virtual Lemonade Stand, a digital project of their own design
These are real, functional outputs, not exercises that disappear when the chapter ends. Many children will want to continue building on them long after the book is finished. Encourage that instinct.
How to Use This Book

The chapters work best read in order. Each one builds on skills introduced in the previous chapters. A child who skips to the Scratch chapter without having read the digital identity chapter hasn't missed plot, but they will have missed the habit-building around organization, intentional saving, and safety awareness that makes the technical chapters land better.

That said, the book is designed to be picked up and put down. If a child is captivated by the art chapter and spends a week making digital drawings before moving on, that's exactly right. Depth over pace.

For classroom or homeschool use: the Facilitator Guide at the back of this book provides chapter-by-chapter discussion questions, extension activities, and safety conversation starters. Each chapter can serve as a one- to three-session unit depending on how deeply you explore each project.

Equipment needed: a computer, tablet, or laptop with internet access. No special software purchases are required. Every tool used in this book has a free version. Scratch (scratch.mit.edu) and Google Sites are both entirely free. Drawing apps with the features described in Chapter 3 include free options like Microsoft Paint, Sketchpad, or the built-in drawing tool in Google Slides. The specific platforms mentioned throughout this book are accurate at time of publication; if an interface has changed, the underlying concepts and steps remain the same.
Your Role as the Trusted Adult
Throughout this book, children are encouraged to talk to a
"trusted adult"
before sharing their work online, before joining new platforms, and whenever something feels wrong. That trusted adult is you.

This book doesn't ask you to become a digital expert. It asks you to be present and reachable, the person your child knows they can bring a question or a concern to without fear of getting in trouble.
A few things worth knowing before you begin:

The Digital Rules Poster project in Chapter 1 is more than a craft activity. It's a conversation starter. Sit with your child as they build it. Discuss what each rule means and why it matters. A poster your child made themselves, with your involvement, carries far more weight than a list of rules you handed them.

The password chapter covers passphrase construction in detail. If your child doesn't yet have passwords of their own to manage, this is a good time to introduce them to your household approach: how your family uses password managers, how accounts are set up, who keeps track of what.

The webpage and video chapters involve publishing to the internet. Both chapters include explicit safety checks before publishing, including privacy settings and personal information review. Work through these checks together the first time. The habits developed here will serve your child for years.

If at any point a chapter raises concerns you want to discuss further (about a platform mentioned, about something your child encountered while working on a project, or about the safety advice itself), the Facilitator Guide at the back of this book includes conversation guides for each chapter's most sensitive topics.
A Note on Screen Time
This book involves screens. The skills it teaches are entirely screen-based. That's not a contradiction of healthy screen habits. It's an invitation to make screen time count.

Creating is categorically different from consuming. A child who spends two hours making a Scratch game has spent those hours problem-solving, debugging, iterating, and building something real. That's qualitatively different from two hours of passive video watching, even though both happen on a screen.

The book includes a section on screen time balance in Chapter 1. It encourages children to sit down with intention, work for a defined period, and then step away. You may want to reinforce this approach, not as a restriction, but as a creative discipline. The best makers, of any age, know when to stop and come back fresh.
A Note on Artificial Intelligence

AI tools (text generators, image makers, coding assistants) are part of the landscape your child is growing up in. This book doesn't dwell on them, because the skills it teaches are more important in an AI-rich world, not less. A child who knows how to code, design, write for an audience, and evaluate what they create is a child who can use AI tools thoughtfully rather than be used by them. The projects in this book build the creative and critical foundation that makes any tool, AI or otherwise, genuinely useful. When your child encounters these tools, and they will, they'll be better equipped because of the work they've done here.
A Note on the Projects
Every project in this book has a
"YOUR QUICK WIN"

label at the chapter opening, a clear statement of what the child will have made by the end of the chapter. This framing is intentional. The promise of a finished product at the end of every chapter keeps young readers motivated through the learning that precedes it.

When a project is finished, acknowledge it. Ask to see the maze game. Read the webpage. Look at the digital drawing. The moment of sharing what they made, with someone who cares, is part of the learning. Don't skip it.
YOUR QUICK WIN: By the end of this chapter, you'll have your digital workspace ready to go and your own Digital Rules Poster, a personal guide to exploring the internet safely and confidently.

The digital world is one of the most extraordinary places you'll ever explore. You can learn how rockets reach space, how to draw a cartoon tiger, or how people lived in ancient Rome, all before lunch. You can create digital paintings, build games, write stories, and share your ideas with people on the other side of the planet. Your curiosity is your compass here. Your creativity is your superpower.

But like any great place, the digital world comes with its own ways of doing things. Think of it like a really cool treehouse. You're thrilled to have it, you want to invite your friends over, and you can't wait to decorate it. But you also know to be careful about who you invite, what you share inside, and how you treat the space, so it stays safe and fun for everyone.

This book is your guide to that treehouse. We'll explore digital art, storytelling, coding, and websites. But first, we'll do two projects: set up your digital workspace so you have a comfortable, organized place to create, and build a Digital Rules Poster, your personal commitment to how you'll use the internet.
Ready? Let's go.
Project 1: Setting Up Your Digital Space

Where you do your digital work matters. A painter has a studio. A musician has a practice room. You need a space that helps you focus and stay comfortable, and setting one up only takes a few minutes.
Pick your spot

Choose somewhere in your home where you can concentrate without too many interruptions. A desk in your bedroom, a corner of the living room, or a spot at the kitchen table all work. The key is consistency: use the same space each time, and your brain learns to switch into creative mode when you sit down there.

Good lighting makes a real difference. Natural light from a window is ideal. When you work in dim light, your eyes strain and tire faster. Position your screen so light isn't shining directly on it. Glare makes it hard to see and gives you headaches.
Set up your body right
Your posture affects how long you can work and how you feel when you're done. Here's a quick checklist:
- Sit with your feet flat on the floor (or resting on something solid if you're shorter)
- Position your screen at eye level or slightly below, not tilted up so you're craning your neck
- Keep your wrists roughly flat when you type, not bent sharply up or down
- Sit back so your back has support
These small things matter when you're building a game or working on a story for an hour. Slouching feels fine for five minutes. Your neck and shoulders will notice it later.
Cut the distractions
Before you start a project, close apps you don't need. Turn off game notifications. Put your phone across the room if it isn't part of the project.
Here's a trick that works: before you open your computer, say out loud what you're going to work on.
I'm going to work on my digital drawing for 45 minutes.
That one sentence sets your intention and makes it much easier to stay on track.
Organize your files from the start
Your computer's storage is like a filing cabinet. Without folders, everything lands in one giant pile and you waste time every time you want to find something.
Create a simple folder structure right now:
My Projects
Art & Design
Stories & Writing
Coding Projects
Schoolwork
Inside each folder, you'll add subfolders as your projects grow. The exact structure doesn't matter as much as having one and sticking to it.
One rule that saves real frustration: name your files clearly.
"Draft1.docx"
tells you nothing a month from now.
"BoltRobotStory_Draft1.docx"
tells you exactly what it is. Start this habit early.
Keep your desktop clear
Your computer's desktop is your work surface. Like a physical desk, it works best when it isn't buried in clutter. Keep only what you're actively using there. Everything else goes in a folder.

Once a week, spend two minutes clearing your Downloads folder. Move what you're keeping to the right folder. Delete what you don't need. This one small habit prevents the digital chaos that makes it hard to find anything.
Keep your software updated
Software updates aren't just new features. They often fix security problems. When your operating system or browser prompts you to update, do it. Updates are your device's immune system.

Your workspace will grow with you. As your skills develop and your projects get more ambitious, your needs will change. The setup you build today is a starting point, not a final answer. The habits you build now (organization, good posture, clear intentions) will serve you no matter how your tools evolve.
Project 2: Your Digital Rules Poster
Now for one of the most important projects in this book.

A Digital Rules Poster is your personal guide for being online. It isn't a list of restrictions. It's a set of commitments you make to yourself about how you'll explore the internet. When you write the rules yourself, you're far more likely to remember and follow them.

You can make your poster on paper with markers and drawings, or create it digitally using a drawing app. Either way, put it somewhere visible: on your wall, next to your monitor, or as your desktop background.
Here's how to build it.
Rule 1: Be Kind Online

Behind every username is a real person. A comment that seems funny to you might land very differently for someone else. Before you type something (a comment on a video, a message in a game, a reply to a post), ask yourself: would I say this to their face?

Being kind online doesn't mean agreeing with everyone or never giving feedback. It means keeping your words respectful even when you disagree. It means not piling on when someone makes a mistake. It means choosing not to share something that would embarrass another person.
For your poster: draw a symbol that means kindness to you: hands reaching out, a smile, a heart. Write
"Be Kind Online"
next to it.
Rule 2: Ask Permission Before Sharing
This rule has two parts.

First: before you share personal information (your full name, your school, your address, your phone number, your location), ask a trusted adult whether it's okay for that particular site. A trusted adult is someone in your real life who looks out for you: a parent, guardian, grandparent, or teacher.

Second: before you share photos or information about anyone else, ask them first. A photo of your friend, their username, their home address. These belong to them. Sharing without permission isn't just rude; it can genuinely hurt people. If you'd want to be asked before something about you was posted, extend that same consideration to others.
For your poster: draw a lock or a shield. Write
"Ask Permission Before Sharing."
Rule 3: Tell a Trusted Adult If Something Feels Wrong
This is the most important rule on your poster.

The internet is enormous, and occasionally you'll encounter something that makes you feel confused, uncomfortable, scared, or upset. This is normal, and it doesn't mean you did something wrong. It means you need help.
Your trusted adults want to know when something doesn't feel right. Telling them isn't tattling. It's exactly the right move. You are never in trouble for speaking up.
What counts as
"something feels wrong"
- Someone online asks for your personal information
- You see content that upsets or confuses you
- Someone asks you to keep secrets from your parents
- An interaction makes you feel pressured, uncomfortable, or scared
Any one of these is a reason to close the app and find your trusted adult immediately.
For your poster: draw a child and a taller figure side by side. Write
"Tell a Trusted Adult If Something Feels Wrong."
Rule 4: Think Before You Click

Not every link or download is safe. Malicious links lead to websites designed to steal information or install harmful software. A simple habit prevents almost all of it: if you don't know where a link leads, don't click it. Ask a trusted adult first.
This rule also covers things that seem too good to be true (
"You've won a prize! Click here!"
) and any files you didn't expect to receive. When in doubt, don't click.
For your poster: draw a magnifying glass over a link. Write
"Think Before You Click."
Rule 5: Be Mindful of My Digital Footprint

Everything you do online leaves a trace. Posts, comments, photos, messages: these can be seen, saved, and shared by others even after you delete them. Your digital footprint is the trail you leave behind.
Before you post anything, ask: would I be comfortable if my teacher saw this? My grandparents? Someone reading it five years from now? If the answer is no, don't post it.
This isn't about being afraid of the internet. It's about being intentional. Your digital footprint is part of your reputation, and you shape it with every choice you make online.
For your poster: draw a footprint. Write
"Be Mindful of My Digital Footprint."
Rule 6: Balance My Screen Time
The internet offers infinite things to explore and create. That's one of its best features, and it also means you have to be the one who decides when to stop.

Healthy digital habits look like this: you sit down knowing what you're going to do and roughly how long you'll spend on it. You take breaks. You put the device away when it's time to eat, sleep, or be present with people around you. You notice when an app or game leaves you feeling irritable or drained, and you step away.
Digital creating matters. The world beyond your screen matters too.
For your poster: draw a clock or a sun with a crescent moon. Write
"Balance My Screen Time."
Building Your Poster
Once you've settled on your rules, make the poster itself.
On paper: Use a large sheet and write each rule as a heading in bold, colorful letters. Draw a symbol next to each one. Decorate the borders. Make it yours.

Digitally: Open a drawing or design program and start a new canvas. Use the text tool for the rules and the drawing tools for your illustrations. Experiment with colors, fonts, and layout. Save it as an image and print it out, or keep it as your wallpaper.
Put it somewhere you'll see it when you sit down to work.

Your poster isn't permanent. As you get older and your online life expands, you'll learn new things about staying safe and being a good digital citizen. Update your rules when something new feels important to add. The goal isn't a perfect document. It's a habit of thinking before you act online.
Chapter 1 Complete
You've done two real things in this chapter: you set up a workspace where you can focus and create, and you made a personal commitment to how you'll use the internet.
Next, we go deeper into your digital identity: how to protect your accounts with strong passwords, how to organize your digital life, and how to control who sees your information online.
Your adventure has started. Let's keep building.
